catalog_locator: Andersen 2007 p. 71, section 6 'Tones', 6.1 'Tone inventory'; loanword-stress remark pp. 80-81; functions of tone sec. 6.6 pp. 81-85; Mayak sentence: Andersen 1999 p. 2 (p. 2).
catalog_quote: 6.1. Tone inventory. Kurmuk is a tone language with three underlying tones: high (H) /ˊ/, low (L) /ˋ/, and a compound falling tone (H͡L) /ˆ/. There are five different surface tones. Three of them are level tones: high (H), downstepped high (ꜜH), and low (L). Two are contour tones, but they are rare, and both of them must be analysed as composed of two level tones: a rise from low to high (L͡H) and a fall from high to downstepped high (H͡ꜜH). At the surface there is no contour tone falling from high to low. [pp. 80-81, on Arabic loans:] ... The syllable in question is the one that bears the stress in the Arabic source words. [Andersen 1999: 2, on Mayak:] Mayak is a tone language, but since I have not yet finished working out its tonal system, my transcription does not include tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only full phonological description of a Northern Burun variety (Kurmuk) treats the language as a three-tone language (H, L, HL underlying; downdrift and downstep) with lexical and grammatical tone, and contains no section, statement or transcription of word stress; the Mayak description likewise calls Mayak a tone language and says nothing about stress. The single occurrence of 'stress' in Andersen 2007 (pp. 80-81) concerns the stressed syllable of Arabic loan sources being reflected as an underlying falling tone in Kurmuk.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is not discussed at all. Loanwords from Arabic (via Berta) carry an underlying HL on the syllable that bears stress in the Arabic source (Andersen 2007: 80-81), which is a tonal, not a stress, statement about Kurmuk.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone (nouns and verbs), with tonal processes (High Spread, Fall Simplification) operating across word boundaries in the phrase; no stress domain is defined. Descriptions are of the Kurmuk (Andersen 2007) and Mayak (Andersen 1999) varieties, both grouped under buru1301 Northern Burun in Glottolog.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog buru1301 'Northern Burun' [bdi] lumps several varieties that Andersen treats as separate languages: Mayak, Kurmuk, Surkum, Regariik (and others; Ecsedy 1973 names eight tribes). The phonology of record (Andersen 2007) describes Kurmuk specifically (data collected in Khartoum 2004 from one principal informant); Andersen 1999 describes Mayak. Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect-level children for buru1301, so both fall under this code. Nothing describes Surkum or Regariik phonology in an opened source.

new_statements.relation_note: Same article and same p. 71 sec. 6.1 passage as the existing statement (which cites it correctly as SAL 36(1), 2007); the Glottolog citation in the works list gives the wrong year and volume (2006, vol. 35). new_statements.rule_in_words: Kurmuk is described as a tone language (H, L, HL underlying; H, ꜜH, L, LH, HꜜH at the surface, with downdrift and downstep). The article has sections on syllable structure, vowels, consonants and tones but no section or sentence on word stress in Kurmuk; the single occurrence of 'stress' (p. 80) concerns the stressed syllable of the Arabic source words of loans, which surfaces in Kurmuk as an underlying falling tone. No statement of stress placement, of non-contrastive stress, or of absence of stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Loanwords from Arabic (some via Berta) carry an underlying HL on the syllable that is stressed in the Arabic source (p. 80-81, exx. 112-113); this is a tonal, not a stress, fact for Kurmuk.
new_statements.identity_note: Andersen 2007 describes Kurmuk specifically (Blue Nile, Sudan), one of the Northern Burun varieties under buru1301 (ISO bdi; Glottolog lists no children). Trommer 2016 is about Mayak, another Northern Burun variety; Andersen 1999 (held by the project from the earlier reading) is also Mayak.

tone_statements.citation: Gilley, Leoma G. 2004. The Lwoian family. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 165-174.
tone_statements.quote: All the Lwoian languages included here have three level tones and at least some have contour tones on short vowels. However, very little is understood about the tonal systems for the most part. ... Thus, we can assume that tone is not so significant at the lexical level, but plays a much more active role at the grammatical level.
tone_statements.summary: Orthography survey: three level tones asserted for all Lwoian languages incl. Burun (Mayak), contour tones on short vowels for 'some'; no tone labels or Burun forms; stress remarks on Shilluk only.
